summary: Describes a TFTP option that lets client and server negotiate a block size better suited to the network medium. It was replaced by RFC 2348.

eli5.summary: Choosing how big each piece of a file is so sending goes faster.

subtitle: Let client and server negotiate larger blocks for faster file transfers.

tldr.problem: TFTP uses 512-byte blocks by default, which is inefficient on modern LANs with much larger MTU sizes. Smaller blocks mean more packets and more overhead.
tldr.mechanism: The blocksize option allows the client and server to negotiate a block size better suited to the network. During the initial request, the client proposes a size; the server responds with an acknowledgment (OACK) specifying the agreed size, which must be 8 to 65464 octets.
tldr.outcome: Larger block sizes reduce transfer time significantly: tests showed 8x faster transfers with 4096-byte blocks compared to 512-byte blocks. This extension was later standardized more formally in RFC 2348.

today: RFC 1783 defined the TFTP blocksize option as a standards-track proposal. It was later replaced and formalized in RFC 2348.

sections.title: TFTP and the Blocksize Problem
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple, lock-step protocol for transferring files. It was originally designed for booting diskless computers from ROM and uses 512-byte blocks, a size chosen for simplicity on resource-constrained machines.

Modern Ethernet and other LANs have MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) sizes of 1500 bytes or larger. The original 512-byte blocksize wastes bandwidth because each block requires an acknowledgment packet, doubling the number of round trips. This document defines a TFTP option to negotiate a larger blocksize better suited to the network medium.
sections.eli5: TFTP was designed for tiny machines and uses tiny 512-byte blocks. Modern networks can carry much bigger pieces, so why not send 4000 bytes at a time instead?

sections.title: The Blocksize Option
sections.content:
The blocksize option is added to the TFTP Read or Write Request packet. The client includes the option name "blksize" and a proposed size (8 to 65464 octets) as null-terminated ASCII strings. For example, a 1432-byte blocksize matches Ethernet MTU minus UDP and IP header lengths.

If the server accepts the option, it sends an Option Acknowledgment (OACK) with a blocksize value less than or equal to the client's proposal. The client must then either use the agreed size or send an ERROR packet to abort.
sections.eli5: The client asks for bigger blocks in its initial request. The server agrees by sending back the size it will use, which is no bigger than what the client asked for.

sections.title: Transfer Speed Improvement
sections.content:
Performance testing on Ethernet with 2.25 MB files showed dramatic improvements. With a 512-byte blocksize, transfers took 23.85 seconds. Increasing to 1432 bytes reduced time to 13.70 seconds (42% faster). A 4096-byte blocksize achieved 6.85 seconds (71% faster), and 8192 bytes reached 4.90 seconds (80% faster).

The speedup comes from fewer packets and acknowledgments. Doubling the blocksize roughly halves the number of packets, and the secondary effect is reduced per-packet framing overhead. However, if the blocksize exceeds the path MTU, IP fragmentation will add overhead, more noticeable with multiple gateways.
sections.eli5: Bigger blocks mean fewer packets, fewer waits for acknowledgments, and less overhead. Tests showed 8x faster transfers with very large blocks.
